metadata.file_name: 127. Sun et al. (2023). A Theoretical Framework for a Mathematical Cognitive Model for Adaptive Learning Systems.pdf
metadata.title: A Theoretical Framework for a Mathematical Cognitive Model for Adaptive Learning Systems

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper does not use an ILSA/PISA/TIMSS micro-dataset for achievement scoring; instead, it constructs a mathematical cognitive model using expert questionnaires, interviews, and student verbal reports. Because the study is based on expert calibration (52 experts) and a small validation activity (one fourth-grade student), there is no complex survey sampling frame and no student-level sampling weights to apply. The ISM procedure uses expert judgments to build a structural self-interaction matrix (SSIM) and then derives adjacency/reachability matrices; these steps are not population-representative estimation. Therefore, standard ILSA weight variables (e.g., student sampling weights or BRR/jackknife replicate weights) are not applicable to the reported model-construction workflow.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not estimate cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA assessment; it develops and validates a theoretical cognitive attribute model using interpretive structural modeling (ISM) and expert/student judgments. The paper also does not report a missing-data strategy because the core inputs are expert questionnaire responses and qualitative/verbal-report validation rather than a PV-based scoring dataset with item nonresponse handled via PV procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses a two-stage cognitive model construction process: (1) 52 experts in Shanghai (33 primary school mathematics teachers, 15 graduate students, and 4 mathematics education specialists) completed a questionnaire to judge pairwise relationships among 16 TIMSS cognitive attributes; (2) six mathematics education professors revised the preliminary model, and a single fourth-grade child was randomly selected to provide an oral verbal report to verify the model’s effectiveness on two extracted TIMSS item types. The paper does not describe any country-level sampling frame or grade-wide student sampling beyond this small validation activity.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This paper proposes a theoretical framework for constructing a mathematical cognitive model intended for cognitive diagnostic assessment and adaptive learning systems. Using TIMSS’s cognitive framework as a starting point, the authors list 16 cognitive attributes (S1–S16) and apply interpretive structural modeling (ISM) to derive hierarchical relationships among attributes via expert judgments. Specifically, 52 experts completed a “cognitive attribute relationship” questionnaire, which was converted into a structural self-interaction matrix (SSIM) using a 50% threshold (more than 25 experts indicating a relationship), followed by adjacency and reachability matrix construction in MATLAB. The preliminary five-level model is then revised using interviews/discussion with six mathematics education professors and validated through verbal reports from one randomly selected fourth-grade student on two TIMSS item types. No predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) are reported because the study’s contribution is model construction and conceptual validation rather than ML-based prediction. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a non-empirical methodology/theory paper focused on constructing a cognitive model using ISM and expert elicitation, not on training/evaluating predictive ML models or estimating PV-based achievement outcomes. As a result, there are no target variables with reported predictive metrics, no PV handling or missing-data handling procedures tied to PV scoring, and no survey-weighted large-scale sampling design to extract.
